title: How to tell whether an automation saved time
metaTitle: Measure automation ROI by the minutes
excerpt: Time the old chore against the minutes spent reviewing the automation. If checking it takes longer than the work did, remove it.
alt: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window. The desk is where someone can time a chore and the review that replaced it.
caption: Minutes are easier to trust when someone writes them down. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How do you tell whether an automation saved time?
faqs.answer: Time the old chore for a normal week, including hunting and retyping. Then time review, repairs, and exceptions on a later boring week, after setup is over. If the review minutes are higher, remove the automation.

faqs.question: What should stay out of the savings figure?
faqs.answer: Leave out the vendor's claimed time, tasks you would not have done by hand, and a subscription you would pay anyway. Include the care and feeding: rule updates, reauthorization, and explaining a wrong output. Give each workflow its own row.

faqs.question: What does a review you can time honestly look like?
faqs.answer: Show the output, the source, and the action that will happen if someone approves. A short check can be timed as judgment. A long report will be skimmed, and a skim does not tell you whether the automation was right.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Measure automation ROI in minutes, on one chore, against the review that chore now requires. Time the old way for a normal week. Time the checking, fixing, and exceptions for the same week after the automation is in. If review takes longer than the chore did, the automation did not save time. Remove it.

A dollar figure can come later, and only if the minutes are real. A platform fee is easy to see. The time a person spends repairing a confident draft is easy to ignore, and that time is the cost.

## Time the old chore before you turn anything on

Pick the workflow you already bounded: one trigger, one output. For five real occurrences, write down the minutes from the moment someone notices the chore to the moment it is done. Include the hunting. Finding the file, opening the right record, retyping the name, sending the reply. Do not include unrelated work that happened to sit nearby.

Five is enough to see the shape. If the times vary wildly, the chore is not one chore. Split it before you automate, or you will compare a machine to a blur.

Write the total for a normal week. "About ten a day, about four minutes each" is a claim you can check. "It feels slow" is not a baseline. Keep the scrap of paper or the note. You will want it when the new tool feels busy and you need the old number.

## Time the review, not the demo

After the automation runs, time what a person still does. Watching the queue. Opening the source. Editing the draft. Handling the cases the rule skipped. Apologizing when it was wrong. Those minutes belong to the automation.

Also time failures honestly. A wrong file sent to a client may cost ten minutes of repair and a longer cost in trust you should not pretend to quantify. Count the repair minutes. Note the trust hit in a sentence beside the table so you do not flatten it into a fake dollar figure.

Compare week to week only after the first frantic days. The first week includes setup, and setup is a cost, but it is not the steady cost. Use a boring week. The question is whether Tuesday is shorter now.

A simple table is enough. Old minutes. Review minutes. Exceptions that still take the old path. If old minutes were 80 and review plus exceptions are 30, you saved time. If they are 90, you added a system and kept the work. Turn it off.

Nielsen Norman Group's research, published by Jakob Nielsen in 2011, is a useful warning about the shape of review, not a benchmark for your chore. Users often leave a web page in 10 to 20 seconds, and they have time to read only about a quarter of the text on pages they do visit. A review packet written like a report will be skimmed. A skim is not a review. If the only way to check the automation is to read a long log, the minutes will lie in the other direction: people will mark it done without looking. Keep the check to the fields that matter, so the timed review is a real one. The article is [How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/).

## What not to count as savings

Do not count the time the tool's marketing claimed. Do not count a task you would not have done by hand anyway. An automated weekly essay nobody read is not a saved hour. It is a new artifact.

Do not spread one chore's savings across the whole company. "We automated" is not a number. The number is attached to the named workflow. If you automate a second one, it gets its own row.

Do not ignore the care and feeding. Updating the rule when a form changes, reauthorizing a connection, and answering "why did it say that" are minutes. If those minutes grow every month, the steady state is worse than the week you measured. Measure again at a month.

A platform subscription is part of the cost only if this workflow is why you pay it. If you would pay for it anyway, leave it out of this comparison so you do not force a bad workflow to justify a bill. If you bought it for this chore, then the minutes saved need to matter to the person who was doing the chore. A fee that buys back ten minutes a week is a poor trade, even when the minutes are real.

## When the result says stop

Stopping is a successful measurement. You learned the output was harder to check than to create, or that exceptions were the real work. Remove the automation, thank the baseline, and choose a different chore or none.

Keep it when the minutes drop and the errors are visible and rare. Then, and only then, consider a second workflow. The second one needs its own baseline. It does not inherit the first one's savings as a story.

Share the table with the person who does the review. If they do not recognize the minutes, you measured the wrong thing. Adjust and time again. A founder looking at a dashboard the operator does not believe will make a confident wrong decision about the tool.

A review surface that can be timed honestly is small. Show the output, the source, and the one action that will happen if they approve. Hide the log of internal steps unless a failure requires it. When the check is a short diff, the minutes you write down are minutes of judgment. When the check is a long page, the minutes include skimming, and skimming does not tell you whether the automation was right.

The chore this measurement assumes is the boring one with a clear input and output. If you do not have that boundary yet, the timing will be noise. Start there: [one boring workflow](/blog/one-boring-automation).

If you want help choosing a chore worth timing, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio would rather retire an automation than defend one that added a queue.
